analysis.one_liner: Gives every U.S. resident the same private health insurance options Members of Congress get.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees and never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor; it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the Office of Personnel Management contract with private insurers to offer the same kind of comprehensive plans federal employees and Members of Congress get, open to every U.S. resident not already in Medicare, Medicaid, or FEHBP. People enrolling when the program started could not be turned down or charged more for preexisting conditions, and premiums could not vary by age, gender, or health status. Members of Congress and the President would have to enroll in this program or the federal employee program, not both.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of uninsured and people with preexisting conditions, who would gain guaranteed access to comprehensive plans with premiums that could not be raised based on their health status; Members of Congress would also be covered by the same program as everyone else.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured people and those with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Opens the program to all U.S. residents who are not already covered by Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, Tricare, or the federal employee program.
Bars plans from excluding or surcharging people for preexisting conditions and health status when they enroll during their initial eligibility period.
Sets premiums under the federal employee program's rating rules so they cannot vary by age, gender, or health status.
Requires plans to match the federal employee benefit package, including preventive benefits such as vaccines, annual physicals, cancer screening, and mental health parity.
Puts Members of Congress and the President into the same program as other residents, allowing enrollment in one or the other plan type but not both.

analysis.who_pays: Enrollees would pay premiums, and employers choosing to move their workers into the program would have to keep paying the same share of premiums they paid before. The text creates no taxpayer subsidies, so people unable to afford premiums would have coverage on paper only; insurers would fund the high-cost reinsurance pool themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Enrollees and employers, with no subsidies

drawbacks.text: The bill sets premiums but never says who pays them for people who cannot afford coverage, providing no subsidies, so universality would depend on ability to pay.
The preexisting-condition protection has a hole: someone who misses the initial enrollment window can be excluded for preexisting conditions at later annual enrollment and pushed to a high-risk pool.
Federal benefit rules would supersede all state insurance laws, wiping out state-mandated benefits and state insurance regulation in one stroke.
An honest supporter would acknowledge the scheme relies on community rating without subsidies, which risks attracting only sick enrollees and driving premiums up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage guarantee for people with preexisting conditions was real and would have mattered to millions. But the bill was a sketch, not a finished law: no financing for people who cannot pay premiums, a loophole for late enrollees, and total preemption of state insurance law. As written, its universality promise would have been uneven in practice.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to four House committees on introduction, then to two subcommittees, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lee Terry introduced the bill on October 27, 2009, during the debate over the Affordable Care Act.
It was referred to four House committees: Energy and Commerce, Oversight and Government Reform, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means.
Within two days it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and in December to the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action was ever taken, and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers were better off: Congress enacted the Affordable Care Act instead, which also expanded coverage by routing millions of new customers through private insurers, and this bill never forced a floor debate on a different model. Members of Congress kept their existing coverage untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, whose market stayed as-is

sides.party_line_note: The only sponsor was a single House Republican and not one member of either party signed on, so no vote ever occurred that would show where each party stood.

industries.note: The bill would make private insurers the permanent channel for universal coverage: OPM would contract with HMOs and group insurers to cover virtually every U.S. resident, giving them a massive new customer base, while imposing guaranteed issue at initial enrollment, community rating, and an insurer-funded reinsurance pool for high-cost patients. Consumers would gain coverage; insurers would gain the market.

Employers could move their workers into the program but would have to keep paying the same share of premiums they paid before, and the workers' coverage would keep its existing tax treatment. It is an option, not a mandate, so the effect is modest in both directions.
